label: Traditional theoretical science fails where irreducibility is present
statement: Traditional theoretical science, including its use of mathematical formulas, relies on computational reducibility, which is the fundamental reason it has made little progress with systems whose behavior is not quite simple and why it has tended to restrict its domain to reducible phenomena.
quote: this, I believe, is the fundamental reason that traditional theoretical science has never managed to get far in studying most types of systems whose behavior is not ultimately quite simple.
scope: theoretical science and mathematical modeling

label: Many common systems can only be understood by explicit simulation
statement: Computer simulation is not merely a convenient substitute for mathematical formulas: there are many common systems whose behavior can be determined only by something like explicit simulation, and there can be no easy theory for almost any behavior that seems complex.
quote: there are many common systems whose behavior cannot in the end be determined at all except by something like an explicit simulation.
scope: common natural and artificial systems with complex behavior

label: Nested cellular automaton patterns can be computed in logarithmic time
statement: For cellular automata with nested behavior such as elementary rules 60 and 188, the color of a cell after t steps can be found in about log2(t) steps from the base-2 digits of its position, rather than by tracing all t steps.
quote: In general, to find the color of a cell after t steps of rule 188 or rule 60 evolution takes about Log[2, t] steps.
scope: elementary cellular automata rules 60 and 188, and nested patterns generally

label: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare
statement: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.
quote: I strongly suspect that systems like this are very rare, and that in the vast majority of cases where the behavior that we see in nature and elsewhere appears to us complex it is in the end indeed associated with computational irreducibility.
scope: systems with complex-looking behavior in nature and among simple programs

label: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation
statement: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.
quote: even though all the components of our brains presumably follow definite laws, I strongly suspect that their overall behavior corresponds to an irreducible computation whose outcome can never in effect be found by reasonable laws.
scope: human brains and other systems that appear to exhibit free will

label: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable
statement: For almost any system whose behavior seems complex, almost any non-trivial question about its behavior after infinitely many steps (e.g. whether a pattern dies out, becomes repetitive, or ever produces a given arrangement) is undecidable, and such undecidability should be widespread in nature.
quote: for almost any system whose behavior seems to us complex almost any non-trivial question about what the system does after an infinite number of steps will be undecidable.
scope: systems with complex behavior, including simple programs and natural systems

label: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions
statement: Undecidability has obvious effects even in a very simple system: in a 4-color totalistic cellular automaton (code 1004600) started from simple initial conditions, some patterns die out only after over a thousand steps while others are still growing after ten million steps with no indication of their final outcome.
quote: undecidability can have quite obvious effects even with a very simple underlying rule and very simple initial conditions.
scope: 4-color totalistic cellular automaton with code 1004600 and simple programs generally

label: Post Correspondence Problem with three pairs is likely undecidable
statement: Whether a set of upper/lower block pairs can be concatenated to give identical strings (the Post Correspondence Problem) is straightforward for two pairs, but already with three pairs there is computational irreducibility, making the question undecidable in general.
quote: I strongly suspect that even with just three pairs there is already computational irreducibility
scope: Post Correspondence Problem instances with small numbers of pairs

label: Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates
statement: Enumerating all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors shows that the maximum number of steps to finish a computation grows with input length only linearly, quadratically, or exponentially, and every exponential case has another such machine computing the same function in bounded steps.
quote: it turns out that the only rates of growth that one ever sees are linear, square and exponential.
scope: all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors, under Wolfram's halting convention

label: Some simple Turing machine computations require exponential effort
statement: Exhaustive search of all roughly 4 billion 4-state 2-color Turing machines shows certain computations by such machines cannot be sped up by any machine of that size, suggesting that some computations specified by very simple rules require effort growing exponentially with input length.
quote: there are indeed Turing machine computations that cannot actually be carried out except by spending an amount of computational effort that can increase exponentially with the length of input.
scope: Turing machines with up to 4 states and 2 colors

label: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts
statement: Almost all the varied systems considered (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution and other systems) can emulate each other in a comparable number of steps, typically with at most polynomial overhead such as t^2 or t^(d+1), so rates of computation do not differ greatly across systems, including presumably those in nature.
quote: almost all the very varied systems in this book can actually be made to emulate each other in a quite comparable number of steps.
scope: cellular automata, Turing machines, register machines, substitution systems and other simple programs

label: P is likely different from NP
statement: It is likely that in most meaningful senses there is no general way to determine whether any path of a multiway or non-deterministic system yields a given outcome in a number of steps growing only polynomially, i.e. P is not equal to NP.
quote: And although it has never been established for certain it seems by now likely that in most meaningful senses there is not.
scope: computational complexity of problems about multiway systems and non-deterministic Turing machines

label: Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete
statement: Even for the rule 30 cellular automaton, deciding whether initial conditions exist that produce a given outcome after t steps (such as a vertical black stripe of a given height in the center column) is expected to be NP-complete, illustrating that simple instances of NP-complete problems are common.
quote: my expectation is that asking about possible outcomes of t steps of evolution will already be NP-complete even for the rule 30 cellular automaton
scope: rule 30 cellular automaton and simple instances of NP-complete problems

label: Quantum computing's exponential speedups are likely an idealization artifact
statement: Although the usual formalism of quantum mechanics allows constructing quantum computers that could solve some problems exponentially faster than ordinary Turing machines, this will likely not reflect ultimate physical reality but only idealizations in current models.
quote: I strongly suspect that even if this is formally the case, it will still not turn out to be a true representation of ultimate physical reality
scope: quantum computation and the fundamental physics of our universe

label: Inverse problems are exponentially harder than forward evolution
statement: In almost any system whose behavior seems complex there is, in a fundamental sense, an almost exponential gap between the effort needed to compute behavior from given initial conditions and the effort needed to determine which initial conditions, if any, produce given behavior.
quote: there really can in some fundamental sense be an almost exponential difference in the amount of computational effort needed to find the behavior of a system with given particular initial conditions, and to solve the inverse problem of determining which if any initial conditions yield particular behavior.
scope: systems with complex behavior, including cellular automata

label: Computational irreducibility makes short theorems with only long proofs inevitable
statement: Because the proof processes of almost every area of mathematics are computationally irreducible, adding axioms cannot remove the problem: there will essentially always be theorems that are short to state but whose shortest proofs are very long.
quote: But I suspect that ultimately there is almost always computational irreducibility, and this makes it essentially inevitable that there will be short theorems that only allow long proofs.
scope: axiom systems of mathematics, idealized as multiway systems

label: An irreducible multiway system cannot be both complete and consistent
statement: If questions about the long-run evolution of a multiway system (an idealized axiom system) are undecidable, then the system cannot be both complete and consistent, because completeness plus consistency would give a procedure that always terminates to decide whether a string is reached.
quote: So the result of this is that if the evolution of a multiway system is computationally irreducible—so that questions about its ultimate behavior are undecidable—the system cannot be both complete and consistent.
scope: multiway systems interpreted as axiom systems with a negation operation

label: Gödel's Theorem follows from the universality of arithmetic, shown via rule 110
statement: An integer (exponential Diophantine) equation can be built whose solutions emulate the rule 110 cellular automaton; since rule 110 is universal, the axioms of arithmetic support universality, which implies Gödel's Theorem that arithmetic contains statements that cannot be proved true or false. Wolfram presents Gödel's Theorem as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
quote: And with the cellular automaton being a universal one such as rule 110 this implies that the axioms of arithmetic can support universality.
scope: axioms of integer arithmetic (Peano arithmetic) and Diophantine encodings of cellular automata

label: Beyond a low threshold almost every axiom system should be universal
statement: The Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that, beyond a low threshold of complexity, almost any axiom system (including very simple ones) should be universal, and so should exhibit undecidability and have no general upper limit on proof length.
quote: And indeed the Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that beyond some low threshold almost any axiom system should be expected to be universal.
scope: all axiom systems, including simple operator and multiway systems

label: Every axiom system used in current mathematical research is universal
statement: Basic logic and pure predicate logic are not universal, but adding a function or relation with more than one argument gives universality; arithmetic, set theory, group theory and ring theory are universal, and every axiom system actually used in current mathematical research is known to be universal, while heavily constrained systems such as commutative group theory and simplified real algebra and geometry are not.
quote: But of the axiom systems actually used in current mathematics research every single one is now known to be universal.
scope: standard axiom systems of mathematics (logic, predicate logic, arithmetic, set theory, group theory, ring theory, real algebra, geometry)

label: Simple integer equations should exist whose lack of solutions is unprovable
statement: Although known universal integer equations are very complicated (the simplest having 9 variables and an immense number of terms), there should be much simpler integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the standard axioms of arithmetic.
quote: so that in fact there are in the end rather simple integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the normal axioms of arithmetic.
scope: Diophantine equations and Peano arithmetic

label: Many open number-theory problems may be unprovable from arithmetic's axioms
statement: A fair fraction of the unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory will turn out to be questions that cannot be answered using the standard axioms of arithmetic.
quote: And it is my strong suspicion that in fact of all the current unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory a fair fraction will in the end turn out to be questions that cannot ever be answered using the normal axioms of arithmetic.
scope: open problems in number theory relative to Peano arithmetic

label: Undecidability appears in almost any area of mathematics beyond easy questions
statement: Undecidability and unprovability will begin to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond questions that are always easy to answer, as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
quote: And indeed from the Principle of Computational Equivalence I strongly believe that in general undecidability and unprovability will start to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond the level of questions that are always easy to answer.
scope: all areas of mathematics

label: Mathematics avoids undecidability by choosing questions its methods can answer
statement: Undecidability and unprovability have seemed rare in mathematics because mathematics, shaped by its history, has defined itself around the questions and systems that proof-based methods can address, concentrating on limited patches of computational reducibility; so present-day mathematics is a small and uncharacteristic sample of what is possible.
quote: it is that like most other fields of human inquiry mathematics has tended to define itself to be concerned with just those questions that its methods can successfully address.
scope: the practice and history of mathematics

label: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated
statement: For a multiway system serving as an axiom system, with negation any length-preserving involution on strings, the system is complete and consistent exactly when half of all possible strings of each length are eventually generated from the string representing true; more than half implies inconsistency and less than half implies incompleteness.
quote: the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half the possible strings of a given length are eventually generated if one starts from the string representing "true".
scope: multiway systems treated as axiom systems with length-preserving negation

label: Axiom systems used in mathematics are usually close to complete
statement: The axiom systems widely used in mathematics, though usually incomplete, are typically close to complete, because they were built to describe definite kinds of objects; as a result, the alternative objects (nonstandard models) that also satisfy them, such as those for standard arithmetic, differ only in obscure ways.
quote: For if one looks at axiom systems that are widely used in mathematics they almost all tend to be complete enough to prove at least a fair fraction of statements either true or false.
scope: standard axiom systems of mathematics such as arithmetic, group theory and set theory

label: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms
statement: Enumerating simple axiom systems for a binary operator shows that the vast majority allow operators of many different forms (many models), so they are not about any one particular operator and are far from complete; only a few, such as those for logic, force essentially a single form.
quote: But what the pictures on the next two pages [804, 805] show is that the vast majority of axiom systems actually allow operators with all sorts of different forms.
scope: simple equational axiom systems for a single binary operator

label: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems
statement: Propositional logic can be axiomatized in terms of Nand by a single axiom with only six Nands (found by searching small axiom systems), far shorter than textbook systems, so an axiom system for logic is likely to be found among the simplest few thousand axiom systems.
quote: So what this means is that if one were just to go through a list of the simplest few thousand axiom systems one would already be quite likely to find one that represents logic.
scope: equational axiom systems for Boolean algebra in terms of Nand

label: Traditional axiom systems are not fundamentally special; others could found new fields
statement: Apart from history, nothing fundamentally distinguishes the axiom systems traditionally used in mathematics (logic included), and many other axiom systems, often simple ones, could serve as foundations for new fields of mathematics as rich as the traditional ones.
quote: So this leads to the conclusion that there is in a sense nothing fundamentally special about the particular axiom systems that have traditionally been used in mathematics
scope: axiom systems underlying fields of mathematics

label: Named textbook theorems of logic are those not derivable from simpler ones
statement: If the theorems of basic logic are listed in order of increasing complexity, the ones that cannot be derived from simpler theorems earlier in the list are almost exactly the ones traditional textbooks single out and name as interesting.
quote: And remarkably enough what I have found is that these theorems are almost exactly the ones highlighted on the previous page that have traditionally been identified as interesting.
scope: theorems of propositional logic and the named laws in logic textbooks

label: Judgments like deep or powerful reflect the structure of the theorem network
statement: Mathematicians' intuitive descriptions of theorems (difficult, powerful, surprising, deep) reflect features of the network of statements connected by theorems, and fields regarded as more successful should have more compact networks while fields full of isolated facts, such as elementary number theory, should have sparser networks.
quote: And my suspicion is that our intuitive characterizations of theorems are in effect just reflections of our perception of various features of the structure of this network.
scope: networks of theorems and proofs in fields of mathematics

label: No general definition of intelligence independent of human details
statement: General features proposed as marks of intelligence (learning and memory, adaptation, abstraction) occur in systems such as simple cellular automata and fluids, so there is no workable general definition of intelligence; any usable one must be tied to specific details of human intelligence.
quote: My guess is that ultimately there is not, and that in fact any workable definition of what we normally think of as intelligence will end up having to be tied to all sorts of seemingly rather specific details of human intelligence.
scope: definitions of intelligence

label: Proposed general features of life occur in many simple-rule systems
statement: Almost any general feature proposed to characterize life, including self-organization, self-reproduction and complexity, occurs even in many systems with very simple rules, so life can only be recognized by specific shared details with life on Earth.
quote: Indeed, following the discoveries in this book I have come to the conclusion that almost any general feature that one might think of as characterizing life will actually occur even in many systems with very simple rules.
scope: definitions of life, terrestrial and extraterrestrial

label: Human artifacts look simple because engineering requires predictability
statement: Human-made artifacts tend to look simpler than natural objects because engineers need to foresee what their systems will do, which requires computational reducibility, whereas nature has no such constraint and many natural systems are computationally irreducible.
quote: And I believe the basic answer to this has to do with the fact that when we as humans set up artifacts we usually need to be able to foresee what they will do—for otherwise we have no way to tell whether they will achieve the purposes we want.
scope: human engineering artifacts compared with natural objects

label: A minimal rule for a feature hints that a system was made for a purpose
statement: Since purposes can always be reinterpreted as mechanisms, purpose cannot be identified for certain from behavior; the best criterion is that a system is the minimal or optimal one producing a given feature, which suggests it was built for that purpose, as advanced technology should increasingly use minimal systems.
quote: finding out that the rule for the system is the minimal or optimal one for producing that feature may make it seem more likely that at least with sufficiently advanced technology the system might have specifically been created for the purpose of exhibiting that feature.
scope: recognizing purpose in artifacts and signals, including extraterrestrial ones

label: Efficient extraterrestrial communications would show no detectable regularities
statement: Signals used for communication by an advanced extraterrestrial civilization would likely be compressed to the point of showing essentially no detectable regularities, so they would look like random radio noise, and searches for sharply defined carrier frequencies would miss them; only beacons meant to be noticed would need recognizable regularities.
quote: my guess is that they will exhibit essentially no detectable regularities. For any such regularity represents in a sense a redundancy or inefficiency that can be removed by the sender and receiver both using appropriate data compression.
scope: extraterrestrial radio signals and searches for extraterrestrial intelligence

label: Sophisticated computation, or primes, are not signs of intelligence
statement: Producing a signal by sophisticated computation is no evidence of intelligence, because such computation is common in ordinary physical processes; for instance, turbulence in the gas around a star quickly does more computation than all of human intellectual history, and sequences such as the primes can be generated by many non-intelligent systems.
quote: And indeed it seems likely that for example an ordinary physical process like fluid turbulence in the gas around a star should rather quickly do more computation than has by most measures ever been done throughout the whole course of human intellectual history.
scope: criteria for detecting extraterrestrial intelligence; natural physical processes

label: Recognizing extraterrestrial intelligence depends on similarity to humans
statement: The difficulty in finding extraterrestrial intelligence is not finding systems that compute in sophisticated ways, which are common, but finding ones whose details are similar enough to humans that we would recognize them as intelligent; somewhat generalized intelligence is likely to exist but to behave in bizarrely unhuman ways.
quote: that the basic issue is not finding systems that perform sophisticated enough computations, but rather finding ones whose details happen to be similar enough to us as humans that we recognize what they do as showing intelligence.
scope: extraterrestrial intelligence

label: Engineering has explored only a tiny unrepresentative fraction of possible systems
statement: Traditional engineering has used only a tiny and unrepresentative fraction of possible systems and processes, those simple enough to predict, and using simple-rule systems with complex behavior will make a vast amount of new technology possible.
quote: And indeed one of the things that emerges from this book is that traditional engineering has actually considered only a tiny and quite unrepresentative fraction of all the kinds of systems and processes that are in principle possible.
scope: engineering and technology

label: Simple universal rules like rule 110 could be built into computers from atoms
statement: Since very simple rules such as the rule 110 cellular automaton are universal, computers could be built from many kinds of components, and a simple chemical process could plausibly assemble a rule 110-like computer at the atomic scale, with one or a few atoms per cell.
quote: For while it is quite implausible that some simple chemical process could successfully assemble a traditional computer out of atoms, it seems quite plausible that this could be done for something like a rule 110 cellular automaton.
scope: molecular and atomic-scale computing technology

label: Exhaustive search is the only reliable way to find programs with given behavior
statement: Because simple programs can do so many unexpected things, and computational irreducibility can make finding a behavior take irreducible work, the only reliable way to find a simple program with a desired behavior is essentially exhaustive search, so building a library of basic knowledge about simple programs is a better route to technology.
quote: ultimately the only way to find what one wants is essentially just to do an exhaustive search of all possibilities.
scope: design of simple programs for technological purposes

label: Humans are not computationally more sophisticated than other systems in nature
statement: By the Principle of Computational Equivalence, human brains, turbulent fluids, simple cellular automata and the universe as a whole all achieve the same level of computational sophistication, so humans are not fundamentally special in intelligence or complexity.
quote: So this means that there is in the end no difference between the level of computational sophistication that is achieved by humans and by all sorts of other systems in nature and elsewhere.
scope: humans, natural systems, simple programs and the universe

label: Computational irreducibility puts permanent limits on scientific prediction
statement: The Principle of Computational Equivalence and computational irreducibility show that science will never predict everything: even if the universe follows simple rules, there is in general no way to know all their consequences except by watching them unfold.
quote: But the Principle of Computational Equivalence—and the phenomenon of computational irreducibility—now shows that this will never happen.
scope: science and knowledge in general

work: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection
label: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection (partial-change form)
statement: The rate of increase in mean fitness of a population due to natural selection equals its additive genetic variance in fitness at that time.
notation: \Delta_{NS}\bar{w} = V_A(w)/\bar{w} (discrete generations); \left.\frac{d\bar{m}}{dt}\right|_{NS} = V_A(m) for Malthusian fitness m
assumptions: the 'partial change' holds average effects of alleles and the environment fixed (Price 1972, Ewens 1989); V_A is the additive genetic variance in fitness.

work: The wave of advance of advantageous genes
label: Fisher-KPP wave of advance of an advantageous gene
statement: An advantageous allele spreading through a continuous population advances as a travelling wave whose speed is set by the selection coefficient and the diffusion (dispersal) rate.
notation: u_t = D u_{xx} + s u(1-u); travelling waves u(x-ct) exist iff c \ge c^* = 2\sqrt{sD}; compactly supported initial data spread at asymptotic speed c^*
assumptions: one spatial dimension (extended to R^n), constant diffusion D, logistic (genic) selection with coefficient s, deterministic large-population limit.

work: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection
label: Fisher's principle of equal investment in the sexes
statement: Under random mating and autosomal inheritance, selection drives parents to invest equally in sons and daughters, which gives a 1:1 sex ratio when the two cost the same.
notation: ESS allocation: N_m c_m = N_f c_f; with c_m = c_f the unbeatable primary sex ratio is 1:1
assumptions: panmixia, autosomal control of the sex ratio, each offspring has one father and one mother, no local mate competition or sex-specific resource competition.

work: The Correlation between Relatives on the Supposition of Mendelian Inheritance
label: Fisher's infinitesimal model of quantitative inheritance
statement: Continuous traits determined by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect produce the observed correlations between relatives, so biometric and Mendelian inheritance are consistent.
notation: Cov(z_i, z_j) = 2\Theta_{ij} V_A + \Delta_{ij} V_D; in the limit of M \to \infty loci the offspring trait given parents is Gaussian with mean (z_1+z_2)/2 and segregation variance V_0(1-\bar{F}), with error O(1/\sqrt{M}) (Barton, Etheridge and Veber 2017)
assumptions: many unlinked loci of small additive effect, random mating, environmental effects independent of genotype.

label: Turing diffusion-driven instability
statement: A homogeneous steady state of two reacting chemicals that is stable without diffusion can become unstable to spatial perturbations when the chemicals diffuse at different rates, spontaneously producing a pattern.
notation:
u_t = f(u,v) + D_u 
abla^2 u, v_t = g(u,v) + D_v 
abla^2 v; with tr J < 0 and det J > 0, instability at some wavenumber k iff D_v f_u + D_u g_v > 2\sqrt{D_u D_v \det J}, which requires D_u 
e D_v
assumptions: two species, smooth kinetics, linearization about a homogeneous steady state, fixed domain without growth or mechanics.

label: Turing wavelength selection
statement: The spacing of a Turing pattern at onset is set by the reaction rates and diffusivities, not by the size of the tissue, so changing these parameters predictably changes the number of repeated elements.
notation: at onset k_c^2 = \sqrt{\det J/(D_u D_v)}, \lambda_c = 2\pi/k_c; under uniform rescaling of D, \lambda \propto \sqrt{D}
assumptions: near onset of instability, two species, domain large compared with the wavelength.

label: Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for biological pattern
statement: Chemical substances that react and diffuse through tissue (morphogens) are sufficient to account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.
notation: no canonical formalization: the claim asserts that a biological pattern is generated by a system of the form u_t = F(u) + D\nabla^2 u with D not proportional to the identity

work: On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population
label: Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele
statement: The probability that a mutant allele eventually fixes in a finite population depends on its initial frequency, its selective advantage and the effective population size, and equals its initial frequency when it is neutral.
notation: u(p) = \frac{1-e^{-4N_e s p}}{1-e^{-4N_e s}}; neutral limit u(p) = p, so a new mutant fixes with probability 1/(2N)
assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, genic (additive) selection with coefficient s, constant effective size N_e, no linkage to other selected sites.

work: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
label: Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate
statement: For neutral mutations the long-run rate of molecular substitution equals the mutation rate per generation, independent of population size, which yields a molecular clock.
notation: k = 2N\mu \cdot \frac{1}{2N} = \mu
assumptions: strictly neutral mutations, mutation rate constant per generation, steady state.

work: The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population
label: Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutant
statement: A neutral mutant that does go to fixation takes on average about four times the effective population size, in generations, to do so.
notation: \bar{t}_1(p) = -\frac{4N_e(1-p)\ln(1-p)}{p}; as p = 1/(2N) \to 0, \bar{t}_1 \to 4N_e generations
assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, neutrality, constant N_e.

work: The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population
label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
statement: Under neutral mutation to new alleles and drift, expected heterozygosity reaches an equilibrium that rises with the product of effective population size and mutation rate.
notation: H = \frac{\theta}{1+\theta}, \theta = 4N_e\mu (infinite-alleles model)
assumptions: infinite-alleles mutation, neutrality, constant N_e, equilibrium.

work: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
label: Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral
statement: Most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly neutral mutations, not by positive selection.
notation: empirical claim: for most sites |N_e s| \lesssim 1, so the fraction of substitutions driven by positive selection \alpha is small; tested with d_N/d_S and McDonald-Kreitman \alpha = 1 - \frac{D_s P_n}{D_n P_s}

work: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I
label: Hamilton's rule
statement: A gene for social behaviour increases in frequency when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the actor.
notation: \Delta \bar{p} > 0 \iff r b - c > 0, with r, b, c defined as regression coefficients (Queller form via the Price equation)
assumptions: in Hamilton's original derivation, additive fitness effects and weak selection; in the general form, b and c are partial regressions of fitness on the actor's and the partner's genotype.

work: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II
label: Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
statement: Because full sisters in haplodiploid species share three quarters of their genes, more than a mother shares with her offspring, haplodiploid insects are predisposed to evolve sterile worker castes.
notation: with a singly mated queen, r_{sister,sister} = 3/4 > r_{mother,daughter} = 1/2, but r_{sister,brother} = 1/4

label: Local mate competition sex ratio
statement: When a few mothers lay eggs on a patch and their offspring mate there before the daughters disperse, the evolutionarily stable sex ratio is female-biased, and the bias weakens as the number of mothers grows.
notation: unbeatable proportion of males x^* = \frac{n-1}{2n} for n foundresses per patch (diploid case)
assumptions: n foundresses per patch, mating confined to the natal patch, only females disperse, mothers control the sex ratio.

work: The moulding of senescence by natural selection
label: Declining force of selection with age
statement: The strength of selection on survival falls with age after reproduction begins, so senescence is an inevitable outcome of natural selection.
notation: s(a) = \frac{\partial r}{\partial \ln p_a} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{x=a+1}^{\infty} e^{-rx} l_x m_x, non-increasing in a
assumptions: an age-structured population with fixed age-specific fertility and no growth or repair after maturity.

label: Evolutionarily stable strategy conditions
statement: A strategy is evolutionarily stable if, once common, it cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.
notation: I is an ESS iff for all J \ne I: E(I,I) > E(J,I), or E(I,I) = E(J,I) and E(I,J) > E(J,J); every ESS is an asymptotically stable rest point of the replicator dynamics (Taylor and Jonker 1978), not conversely
assumptions: an infinite, well-mixed population with pairwise interactions and asexual or clonal inheritance of strategies.

work: Evolution and the Theory of Games
label: Hawk-Dove mixed ESS
statement: When the cost of injury exceeds the value of the contested resource, the stable outcome is a mixture in which animals escalate with probability equal to the ratio of resource value to injury cost.
notation: payoffs E(H,H) = (V-C)/2, E(H,D) = V, E(D,H) = 0, E(D,D) = V/2; for C > V the unique ESS plays Hawk with probability p^* = V/C
assumptions: symmetric pairwise contests, fixed V and C, no role asymmetries (asymmetries such as ownership give the Bourgeois ESS instead).

work: The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts
label: War of attrition ESS
statement: In contests settled by display, where the animal willing to persist longer wins and costs grow with time, the stable strategy is to choose a persistence time at random from an exponential distribution whose mean equals the resource value.
notation: with cost linear in time at unit rate and resource value V, the ESS persistence time has density p(x) = \frac{1}{V} e^{-x/V}
assumptions: symmetric contests, cost linear in display time, no information about the opponent's choice.

label: Twofold cost of sex
statement: An asexual mutant female in a sexual population with equal sex ratio produces twice as many grandchildren as a sexual female, so sex needs a compensating advantage of up to twofold to persist.
notation: with equal fecundity and a 1:1 sex ratio, the odds of asexual to sexual females double each generation: \frac{q_{t+1}}{1-q_{t+1}} = 2\frac{q_t}{1-q_t}
assumptions: anisogamy with males contributing no resources, equal fecundity and viability of sexual and asexual females, a 1:1 sex ratio.

work: The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene
label: Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)
statement: When a favourable mutation sweeps to fixation, it reduces genetic variation at closely linked neutral sites, and the reduction is larger the tighter the linkage relative to the strength of selection.
notation: the relative heterozygosity H_{after}/H_{before} at a neutral site at recombination fraction c is an increasing function of c/s that tends to 0 as c/s \to 0; the affected region has a width of order s in recombination units, up to logarithmic factors in N
assumptions: a single sweep from a new mutation, deterministic allele-frequency trajectory, two loci.
